title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
tagline: From owned servers to on-demand infrastructure — the service models, global topology, and economic shift that define modern cloud.

sections.content:
In 2006, Amazon released a public API that let anyone rent a virtual server by the hour and turn it off when they were done. The name — Elastic Compute Cloud, or EC2 — contained the central promise: elastic. Before that moment, launching a product meant writing purchase orders, waiting six to eight weeks for hardware delivery, racking servers in a data center, configuring networking, and then paying for that peak capacity whether you used it or not. A traffic spike on launch day could melt your infrastructure. A quiet month still billed the full co-location lease.

**Cloud computing** is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases, networking, and higher-level services over the internet, with pay-per-use pricing. The word 'cloud' is just a metaphor for 'someone else's data center you access over the internet' — but the implications are profound. Three major providers now operate at planetary scale: **AWS** (Amazon Web Services), **Google Cloud Platform (GCP)**, and **Microsoft Azure**. Together they run hundreds of data centers on every continent, organized into geographic **regions** and fault-isolated **availability zones**, and they sell access to those resources in three layered models: **IaaS**, **PaaS**, and **SaaS**.

Understanding cloud fundamentals is not optional for modern engineers. Every startup ships on cloud. Every enterprise is migrating to cloud. The design decisions — which service model, which region, which managed service, how to handle identity and access — determine the security, cost, and reliability of everything running on top. This chapter builds those foundations from the ground up: why cloud exists, how it is structured geographically, what the service models actually mean for your day-to-day engineering, how the economics work, who is responsible for what under the shared responsibility model, and how to reason about data residency, latency, and fault tolerance when architecting a real system.

sections.title: Pizza as a Service
sections.content:
The classic analogy works because everyone understands pizza. **On-premises** is making pizza at home: you bought the oven, sourced the flour and toppings, preheated, baked, and cleaned up. You control every ingredient and every step, but you also shoulder every responsibility. **IaaS** is ordering a ready-to-bake pizza kit: the dough and sauce arrive pre-made (the server is provisioned), but you still operate the oven (manage the OS, runtime, and patches) and do the baking. **PaaS** is delivery from a pizzeria: you chose the toppings (your application code) and they handled the entire kitchen — the dough recipe, the oven temperature, the staffing. You do not care how the kitchen works; you get a finished pizza. **SaaS** is dining at a restaurant: you simply eat (use the application). Someone else handles ingredients, kitchen, waitstaff, and dishes.

The higher you go in the service stack, the less time you spend on undifferentiated heavy lifting and the more time you spend on what makes your product unique. The trade-off is control: the restaurant does not let you redesign their kitchen. In engineering terms, higher service models mean faster deployment and less operational burden, but less ability to tune the underlying environment.

sections.title: IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service
sections.content:
**IaaS** is the foundational layer: rented virtual machines, block storage, load balancers, and raw networking, delivered on demand. The cloud provider manages the physical hardware, the network fabric connecting it, and the **hypervisor** — the software layer that carves physical servers into isolated virtual machines. You receive a virtual machine and manage everything from the operating system upward.

The archetypal IaaS product is **AWS EC2** (Elastic Compute Cloud). You choose an AMI (Amazon Machine Image — a disk snapshot of an OS), an instance type (`t3.micro`, `m6i.4xlarge`), a VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) and subnet, and security groups (stateful firewall rules). Within minutes you have a Linux or Windows machine with a public IP address. You SSH in, install your runtime, deploy your code, and configure your own monitoring. You are responsible for OS patches, security hardening, disk backups, and scaling.

The equivalent products on other providers are **Google Compute Engine (GCE)** and **Azure Virtual Machines**. All three follow the same model: the provider secures the physical layer; you own the guest OS and everything running on it.

**Why choose IaaS?** When you need maximum control — custom kernel parameters, specific OS versions, GPU drivers, software that cannot run in a managed environment — IaaS is the right choice. Legacy applications that assume direct hardware access also land naturally on IaaS. The cost is operational complexity: you need to patch, monitor, and scale manually (or build automation to do so).

**Block storage** is IaaS's sibling service. AWS EBS (Elastic Block Store), GCP Persistent Disk, and Azure Managed Disks attach network-backed storage volumes to VMs. Unlike local SSDs, block volumes persist independently of the VM lifecycle — you can detach from one instance and reattach to another, a critical property for stateful workloads.

sections.title: PaaS — Platform as a Service
sections.content:
**PaaS** inserts a managed runtime between you and the infrastructure. You push application code (or a container image); the platform handles OS updates, runtime version management, auto-scaling, health checks, load balancing, and deployment pipelines. You focus entirely on your application logic.

**Heroku** is the classic PaaS: `git push heroku main` and your Node.js or Python app is deployed, scaled, and served — no Nginx configuration, no systemd unit files, no OS patching. Google App Engine and AWS Elastic Beanstalk offer similar models on their respective clouds.

Modern PaaS has evolved significantly. **Container-based PaaS** (AWS ECS, GCP Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps) lets you bring a Docker image and have the platform handle scheduling, scaling, and networking. **Serverless functions** (AWS Lambda, GCP Cloud Functions, Azure Functions) take this further: you upload a function handler; the platform provisions compute only when a request arrives, charges per invocation, and scales to zero when idle. The distinction between PaaS and FaaS (Function as a Service) matters architecturally — Lambda is event-driven and stateless by design, while App Engine or Elastic Beanstalk hosts long-running HTTP servers.

**Managed databases** are a critical PaaS subcategory. AWS RDS, GCP Cloud SQL, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL handle OS patching, engine version upgrades, automated backups, point-in-time recovery, replication, and failover. You provision a PostgreSQL or MySQL instance and connect to it with a standard connection string — the database administration work disappears. The trade-off: you cannot access the underlying OS, cannot install arbitrary PostgreSQL extensions not supported by the managed service, and cannot tune OS-level kernel parameters.

**When to choose PaaS**: Teams that want to ship fast without a dedicated operations function benefit enormously from PaaS. Startups, internal tools, microservices with standard runtime requirements, and event-driven workloads are natural fits. The rule of thumb: default to PaaS; drop to IaaS only when you hit a specific limitation PaaS cannot satisfy.

sections.title: SaaS — Software as a Service
sections.content:
**SaaS** is the topmost abstraction: a finished application delivered over the internet. Gmail, Slack, Salesforce, GitHub, Figma, and Notion are all SaaS. You log in, configure the application to your needs, and use it. You manage nothing below the application layer — not the OS, not the runtime, not the database engine, not the servers.

From an engineering perspective, SaaS is what you build for your customers. But engineers also consume SaaS as infrastructure: using Datadog for observability, PagerDuty for alerting, Twilio for SMS, SendGrid for email, Stripe for payments. These are all SaaS products that expose APIs, and integrating them is faster than building equivalent functionality yourself.

The business model that makes SaaS viable is **multi-tenancy**: a single deployment serves thousands or millions of customers. Your data is logically isolated (by tenant ID in the database, by IAM policy on object storage) even though you share the same underlying infrastructure as everyone else. This pooling of resources is what allows SaaS providers to offer competitive pricing while investing in uptime, security, and features at a scale no individual customer could afford alone.

**The blurring of models**: In practice, lines blur. AWS Lambda is technically PaaS (you manage the function code) but is often called FaaS. Kubernetes on AWS (EKS) is IaaS (you control the cluster) but comes with managed control planes. 'Serverless' is a marketing term that describes managed execution environments where you pay per request, not per idle server — it spans both PaaS and FaaS depending on the product.

sections.title: Global Topology — Regions and Availability Zones
sections.content:
Cloud providers do not operate a single massive data center — that would be a single point of failure and would create unacceptable latency for users on the other side of the planet. Instead, they organize infrastructure into a two-level geographic hierarchy: **regions** and **availability zones**.

A **region** is a geographic cluster of data centers — a distinct physical area of the world. AWS as of 2024 operates 33 regions: `us-east-1` (Northern Virginia), `eu-west-1` (Ireland), `ap-southeast-1` (Singapore), and so on. GCP calls them 'regions' too (`us-central1`, `europe-west1`); Azure calls them 'regions' but names them differently (`East US`, `West Europe`). Each region is operationally independent: a power grid failure in one region does not affect another.

Within each region, an **availability zone (AZ)** is a physically separate data center (or a tight cluster of buildings) with its own power supply, cooling, and network connections. AZs within a region are connected to each other by dedicated, low-latency private fiber — typically sub-millisecond round-trip times. AWS regions have two to six AZs each. AZ names look like `us-east-1a`, `us-east-1b`, `us-east-1c`.

The key insight is that **AZ failures are independent**. A fire in `us-east-1a` does not affect `us-east-1b`. A bad software deployment to one AZ's power management system does not cascade to others. This allows architects to design for **high availability**: distribute application instances across multiple AZs, and if one AZ goes down, the others continue serving traffic. The load balancer detects the unhealthy AZ and routes around it automatically.

**Region selection criteria** — choosing the wrong region has permanent consequences:
1. **Regulatory and data residency requirements** come first. GDPR requires EU personal data to stay in EU regions. HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and country-specific laws may mandate specific certified regions.
2. **Latency to end users** comes second. Physics is undefeatable: light travels at ~200 km/ms in fiber. A user in Tokyo gets lower latency from `ap-northeast-1` than from `us-east-1`.
3. **Service availability**: not every cloud service is available in every region. Some newer or specialized services launch in `us-east-1` first.
4. **Pricing**: AWS and GCP prices vary by region, sometimes by 10-20%.

**Edge locations** (AWS CloudFront POPs, GCP Cloud CDN, Azure CDN) are a third tier: dozens or hundreds of lightweight caching nodes positioned in cities around the world, closer to end users than full regions. CDN edge nodes cache static content and some API responses, reducing latency for the last mile without requiring a full regional deployment.

sections.title: The Shared Responsibility Model
sections.content:
One of the most misunderstood aspects of cloud computing is **who is responsible for what**. The shared responsibility model draws a clear line: the cloud provider secures the infrastructure; you secure what runs on it.

**What the provider always secures**: Physical data center security (guards, cameras, biometrics, man-traps), the network hardware (switches, routers, fiber), the physical servers (host OS, hardware maintenance), and the hypervisor (the virtualization layer that isolates VMs from each other). On managed services like RDS or S3, the provider also manages the software stack up to the service boundary — OS patches for RDS instances, replication for S3 objects.

**What you always own**: IAM (Identity and Access Management) policies — who can assume which roles and access which resources. Data encryption — whether your S3 buckets are encrypted at rest and your traffic is encrypted in transit. Application code and its dependencies. Security group rules — the virtual firewall controlling which ports accept traffic. Network ACLs. Monitoring and alerting for your application.

**The IaaS exception**: On EC2, you additionally own the guest OS. AWS manages the hypervisor; you manage the Linux or Windows instance running on top. That means you must apply OS patches, configure `sshd`, harden the OS, manage users, and monitor process-level metrics. This is a major operational burden that PaaS and SaaS eliminate.

**Why this matters in practice**: The majority of cloud security incidents are customer-caused, not provider-caused. An S3 bucket misconfigured as public, an IAM role with `*:*` permissions attached to a compromised EC2 instance, an unpatched Apache Struts installation on an EC2 instance — all of these are the customer's responsibility. The Equifax breach (2017), the Capital One breach (2019), and many others exploited misconfigurations in the customer's domain, not flaws in the provider's physical infrastructure.

A practical mnemonic: **'The cloud provider secures the cloud; you secure what's in it.'**

sections.title: Cloud Economics — Pay-as-you-go and the CapEx/OpEx Shift
sections.content:
The economic model of cloud computing is as transformative as the technology itself. Traditional IT is **capital expenditure (CapEx)**: large upfront purchases of servers, networking equipment, software licenses, and data center space, written off over multi-year depreciation schedules. You buy for peak load, which means most of the time your expensive hardware sits partially idle.

Cloud converts infrastructure to **operational expenditure (OpEx)**: you pay for what you use, billed by the second or minute, on a credit card or invoice. No procurement cycles, no depreciation schedules, no hardware going obsolete in your rack. An EC2 `t3.medium` costs approximately $0.0416/hour. Running 100 of them for a two-hour load test costs about $8.32 — then you terminate them and pay nothing more. Purchasing 100 physical servers for a two-hour test would cost tens of thousands of dollars.

**Pricing dimensions** in cloud are numerous and can surprise teams:
- **Compute**: per-second billing for EC2, per-invocation for Lambda, per-vCPU-second for Cloud Run.
- **Storage**: per GB-month for S3, EBS, and managed databases — data at rest is not free.
- **Network egress**: data leaving the cloud (to the internet or to another region) costs money. Ingress (data coming in) is typically free. This asymmetry creates **data gravity** — it becomes expensive to move large datasets out of a provider, making migration harder over time.
- **API requests**: S3 charges per PUT/GET request in addition to storage. DynamoDB charges per read/write capacity unit.
- **Managed service overhead**: RDS costs roughly 2-3× more than a self-managed EC2 instance with the same specs — you pay a premium for the managed experience.

**Reserved Instances and Savings Plans**: Pay-as-you-go is most expensive for predictable baseline workloads. AWS, GCP, and Azure offer 1-year or 3-year commitments at discounts of 30-60%. A team with stable compute needs (web servers that always run) should commit; teams with spiky or unpredictable load benefit from on-demand pricing.

**Spot Instances (AWS) / Preemptible VMs (GCP)**: Cloud providers sell unused capacity at 60-90% discount, with the caveat that they can reclaim the instance with 2 minutes notice. Fault-tolerant batch workloads (ML training, genomics pipelines, video encoding) are ideal candidates. Stateless web tier instances can also use spot with careful architecture.

**The elasticity benefit**: Beyond cost, elasticity changes what is architecturally possible. A media company streaming a major sports event can provision 10,000 servers for 4 hours, then release them. Before cloud, that would have required owning 10,000 servers that sat idle 99% of the year.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# AWS CLI — provision resources and observe the service model in action

# IaaS: launch a raw EC2 virtual machine (you manage the OS from here)
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c02fb55956c7d316 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --key-name my-keypair \
  --security-group-ids sg-0abc123def456789 \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abc123 \
  --region us-east-1
# Result: a VM with a public IP. SSH in and configure everything yourself.

# PaaS: deploy code to Elastic Beanstalk (no OS management required)
eb init my-app --platform "Node.js 18" --region us-east-1
eb create my-env
eb deploy   # push code; EB handles scaling, health checks, OS patches

# List regions to understand global topology
aws ec2 describe-regions \
  --query 'Regions[].RegionName' \
  --output table

# List AZs within a region
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'AvailabilityZones[].ZoneName'
# Output: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c", "us-east-1d", "us-east-1e", "us-east-1f"]

# Create an S3 bucket (object storage — the cloud's workhorse)
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket my-unique-bucket-name-2024 \
  --region us-east-1

# Block ALL public access (critical security baseline — never skip this)
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket my-unique-bucket-name-2024 \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
    "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"
sections.explanation: IaaS (`run-instances`) gives you a raw VM — you SSH in and configure it. PaaS (`eb deploy`) accepts your code and handles all infrastructure concerns. The S3 commands illustrate two key lessons: (1) object storage is a cloud primitive you will use constantly; (2) blocking public access should be the default — not the exception. Many security incidents trace back to teams forgetting this step.

sections.title: Core Cloud Services — The Building Blocks
sections.content:
Beyond the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS classification, every major cloud provider offers a set of core primitive services that architects combine to build systems:

**Compute**: Virtual machines (EC2/GCE/Azure VMs), managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS), serverless functions (Lambda/Cloud Functions/Azure Functions), container runtimes (ECS/Cloud Run/Azure Container Apps).

**Object Storage**: AWS S3, GCP Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage. Object storage is flat — no directories, just key-value pairs (path → bytes). It is infinitely scalable, highly durable (AWS S3 promises 99.999999999% — 'eleven nines' — annual durability via cross-AZ replication), and cheap (~$0.023/GB-month for S3 Standard). It is the universal store for static assets, backups, data lake files, ML training datasets, and application artifacts.

**Managed Relational Databases**: AWS RDS and Aurora, GCP Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL. The managed database tier eliminates the need to run your own PostgreSQL or MySQL on an EC2 instance — the provider handles failover, backups, patching, and replication.

**NoSQL and Specialized Databases**: DynamoDB (AWS key-value/document at any scale), Cloud Firestore (GCP), Cosmos DB (Azure). Redis-compatible caches (ElastiCache, Memorystore). Search (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch managed). Time-series databases. The cloud provider offering managed versions of these services shifts maintenance work from your team to the provider.

**Networking primitives**: **VPC** (Virtual Private Cloud) — a private, software-defined network within the cloud where you control IP address ranges, subnets, routing tables, and internet gateways. **Security Groups** — stateful firewalls attached to resources. **NAT Gateways** — allow private-subnet resources to reach the internet without being directly reachable. **Load Balancers** — distribute traffic across instances; Application Load Balancers operate at Layer 7 (HTTP) and can route by path or hostname.

**Identity and Access Management (IAM)**: Every cloud resource has a permission model. AWS IAM lets you create **users** (humans), **roles** (assumed by services, Lambda functions, EC2 instances), and **policies** (JSON documents expressing what actions on which resources are allowed or denied). The principle of least privilege — grant only the minimum permissions required — is the single most impactful security practice in cloud.

**CDN**: AWS CloudFront, GCP Cloud CDN, Azure CDN. Content Delivery Networks sit in front of your origin (S3, load balancer, etc.) and cache responses at edge nodes close to users. Static websites, images, video, and cacheable API responses all benefit. CloudFront also provides DDoS protection (AWS Shield) and WAF (Web Application Firewall) integration.

  physical_security:
    - "Data center buildings, fences, security personnel"

    - "EKS: Kubernetes control plane availability"

  always_yours:

    - "Data encryption at rest (KMS key management)"
    - "Data encryption in transit (TLS certificates, HTTPS enforcement)"
    - "Application code, dependencies, and their CVEs"

  - "IAM roles with '*:*' wildcard permissions"

sections.explanation: The YAML structure makes the responsibility boundary visible. Every item in `customer_responsibility` represents a real-world attack surface. The `common_customer_mistakes` list reflects actual breach post-mortems — these are not theoretical. A robust cloud security posture starts by working through each item methodically.

sections.title: Designing for High Availability and Fault Tolerance
sections.content:
Cloud does not automatically make your application highly available — you must design for it explicitly. The cloud provides the building blocks; the architecture determines the resilience.

**The failure model**: In cloud, hardware failures are not exceptional events — they are expected. Any individual VM can be terminated at any time (hardware failure, hypervisor migration, spot reclamation). Network partitions between services are possible. Managed services (RDS, DynamoDB) occasionally have elevated error rates during maintenance windows. A resilient cloud architecture treats failure as a constant low-probability event happening across thousands of instances, not a rare catastrophe.

**Stateless application tier**: The primary pattern for high availability is to make web/application servers stateless. No in-memory session state, no local disk state — all state lives in a shared backing store (database, Redis, S3). Stateless servers can be terminated and replaced by an Auto Scaling Group at any time, spread across multiple AZs, and load-balanced without coordination.

**Multi-AZ database**: For relational databases, use Multi-AZ deployment (AWS RDS Multi-AZ, GCP Cloud SQL HA, Azure Zone-Redundant). The primary and standby run in separate AZs, with synchronous replication. Failover is automatic (typically 30-60 seconds). Without Multi-AZ, a single AZ failure takes your database offline until the AZ recovers.

**Health checks and Auto Scaling**: Application Load Balancers continuously health-check each instance on a configurable endpoint (e.g., `GET /health`). Unhealthy instances are removed from the target group immediately. Auto Scaling Groups replace terminated instances and add new ones during traffic spikes. Together, these two mechanisms provide both fault recovery and elasticity.

**Multi-region** goes further: deploying the entire stack (application, database, CDN) in two or more regions, with traffic routing based on latency or failover (Route 53 health-checked failover, GCP Traffic Director). Multi-region architecture defends against regional disasters — a full region outage — and can also dramatically reduce global latency by serving users from the nearest region. The complexity cost is significant: cross-region data replication, eventual consistency trade-offs, and substantially higher operational overhead.

**Recovery objectives**: Architects talk about **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective — how long can the system be down during a failure) and **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective — how much data loss is acceptable). A Multi-AZ RDS setup gives RTO of ~60 seconds and RPO of ~0 (synchronous replication = no data loss). A single-AZ setup with daily snapshots gives RTO of hours and RPO of 24 hours. The architecture must match the business requirement.

sections.title: Serverless Computing — The Logical Endpoint
sections.content:
**Serverless** is a confusing term because servers are absolutely involved — you just never see or manage them. Serverless computing means you write function-level code, upload it to the provider, and the platform handles every infrastructure concern: provisioning a container, routing the request, executing your code, scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and billing you for execution time at millisecond granularity.

**AWS Lambda** is the canonical example. A Lambda function is a handler: `exports.handler = async (event) => { ... }`. You specify the runtime (Node.js 20, Python 3.12, Go, Java), the memory allocation (128 MB to 10 GB — CPU scales proportionally with memory), and a timeout (up to 15 minutes). Lambda supports hundreds of event sources: API Gateway (HTTP), S3 events (file uploaded), SQS messages, DynamoDB streams, EventBridge rules (cron).

The serverless economics are compelling for spiky workloads: Lambda costs $0.0000002 per invocation plus $0.0000166667 per GB-second. A function consuming 256 MB and running for 200 ms costs $0.00000083 per invocation. One million invocations costs $0.83. A moderately trafficked API running on Lambda can cost less per month than a single EC2 instance.

The **cold start** problem is the primary serverless limitation. When Lambda initializes a new execution environment (first request, scaling event, after a period of inactivity), it must download your deployment package, start the runtime, and run your initialization code before handling the request. This adds latency — typically 100 ms to 2 seconds depending on runtime and package size. Subsequent requests on the same 'warm' execution environment reuse the process and have no cold start penalty. For user-facing APIs where latency consistency matters, this is a meaningful consideration. Solutions: keep functions warm with scheduled pings, use Provisioned Concurrency (pre-warmed execution environments at extra cost), minimize deployment package size, prefer lightweight runtimes (Node.js/Python over Java for cold-start sensitivity).

**Serverless is not always cheaper**: For constant, high-throughput workloads (thousands of requests per second, 24/7), EC2 or containers with reserved capacity can be significantly cheaper than per-invocation Lambda pricing. Serverless wins on spiky, irregular, or event-driven workloads.

**A brief history of cloud**: The concept of time-shared computing dates to the 1960s — John McCarthy proposed in 1961 that computing could be organized as a public utility. Salesforce launched as a SaaS CRM in 1999. AWS S3 launched in March 2006; EC2 followed in August 2006 — these two services created the modern cloud market. Google App Engine launched in 2008 (PaaS). Microsoft Azure launched in 2010. AWS Lambda launched in 2014, establishing the serverless paradigm. Today AWS alone generates over $90 billion in annual revenue, making cloud infrastructure one of the most profitable technology businesses ever built.

**Interview and exam points to nail:**
- **IaaS vs PaaS boundary**: IaaS = you manage the OS. PaaS = provider manages OS and runtime. This line is where most interview questions focus.
- **Shared responsibility**: The phrase 'security OF the cloud vs. security IN the cloud' (AWS's own framing) instantly clarifies who owns what.
- **Multi-AZ vs. Multi-Region**: Multi-AZ handles hardware/data center failures (same geographic area, sub-second failover). Multi-Region handles regional disasters or global latency (different geography, more complex).
- **S3 durability vs. availability**: 11-nines durability = data is not lost. 99.99% availability = service is accessible. These are different SLAs. An S3 object can be durable (not lost) but temporarily unavailable (service error).
- **Data egress costs**: A classic systems design trap. Moving data OUT of a cloud region or to the internet costs money ($0.09/GB for AWS to internet). Design data flows carefully — cross-region replication and CDN offload can reduce egress bills significantly.

items: **IaaS** provides raw virtual machines and networking — you manage the OS and everything above the hypervisor. Maximum control, maximum operational burden. Use for custom environments, legacy apps, and GPU workloads.

**PaaS** provides a managed runtime where you deploy code without managing servers, OS patches, or scaling. Managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) are a critical PaaS subcategory that eliminates database administration overhead.
**SaaS** delivers finished applications — you configure, not operate, the underlying infrastructure. Engineers both consume SaaS (Stripe, Datadog, Twilio) and build it for customers.

**Regions** are independent geographic clusters of data centers; **Availability Zones** are physically separate data centers within a region. Multi-AZ deployments survive hardware failures; multi-region deployments survive regional disasters.

**Shared responsibility**: the cloud provider secures physical hardware and the hypervisor layer; you own IAM policies, data encryption, security group rules, application code, and — for IaaS — the guest OS.

**Pay-as-you-go** converts capital expenditure to operational expenditure. Elasticity enables burst capacity (millions of users) and ephemeral resources (load tests, batch jobs) at costs impossible with owned hardware. Watch egress fees and idle resource costs.

**Serverless** (Lambda, Cloud Functions) eliminates server management entirely — you pay per invocation at millisecond granularity. Ideal for event-driven and spiky workloads; cold starts are the primary trade-off to architect around.

quiz.question: A company wants to run a custom Linux application requiring specific kernel parameters and full OS-level control. Which cloud service model fits best?
options: SaaS — fastest to deploy with no infrastructure management
PaaS — managed runtime removes OS management burden
IaaS — raw virtual machines with full guest OS access
FaaS — serverless functions with no server management
quiz.explanation: IaaS provides virtual machines where the customer manages the guest OS, runtime, kernel parameters, and everything above the hypervisor. PaaS and SaaS abstract away OS access entirely.

quiz.question: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system on an EC2 instance?
options: AWS — they manage all server software including the guest OS
The customer — they control everything above the hypervisor on EC2
Both share this equally, applying patches together on a schedule
The OS vendor (e.g., Canonical for Ubuntu) pushes patches automatically
quiz.explanation: AWS manages the physical hardware and hypervisor. For EC2 (IaaS), the customer owns the guest OS, which includes applying security patches, hardening the OS, and managing users. This is explicitly the customer's responsibility.

quiz.question: What is the PRIMARY purpose of deploying an application across multiple Availability Zones in the same region?
options: To reduce latency for global users by serving from the closest AZ
To lower costs by distributing load across cheaper AZs
To survive a single data-center failure without causing downtime
To meet the distributed systems requirement of having 3 replicas
quiz.explanation: AZs are physically separate data centers with independent power, cooling, and network connections. A hardware failure, fire, or power outage in one AZ does not affect others in the same region. Multi-AZ deployment provides high availability against data-center-level failures.

quiz.question: Heroku, Google App Engine, and AWS Elastic Beanstalk are examples of which service model?
options: IaaS — infrastructure as a service providing raw virtual machines
SaaS — software as a service delivering finished applications
PaaS — platform as a service providing a managed application runtime
FaaS — function as a service for event-driven serverless workloads
quiz.explanation: PaaS platforms accept application code and handle the runtime, OS, scaling, health checks, and deployment pipeline. Developers push code without managing servers. Heroku, App Engine, and Elastic Beanstalk all fit this model.

quiz.question: Which factor should be considered FIRST when selecting a cloud region for an application that handles EU personal data?
options: Latency to the majority of end users
Pricing differences between available regions
Data residency and regulatory requirements such as GDPR
Number of available instance types and managed services in the region
quiz.explanation: GDPR and similar regulations require EU personal data to remain within specific geographic boundaries. Regulatory compliance is non-negotiable and takes precedence over latency or cost optimizations. Choosing the wrong region for compliance reasons requires painful data migration later.

quiz.question: Cloud pay-as-you-go pricing primarily transforms infrastructure spending from:
options: Variable cost to fixed cost, providing budget predictability
Capital expenditure (CapEx) to operational expenditure (OpEx)
Monthly billing cycles to annual prepaid contracts
Per-physical-server pricing to per-user seat pricing
quiz.explanation: Owning servers is capital expenditure — large upfront cost depreciated over years. Cloud pay-as-you-go converts this to OpEx: ongoing operational cost that scales with usage. This eliminates idle capacity cost and removes the procurement bottleneck for new infrastructure.

quiz.question: What does AWS S3's 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability guarantee specifically describe?
options: The uptime availability of the S3 service API endpoint per year
The probability that a stored object will NOT be lost or corrupted over one year
The latency guarantee for object retrieval under normal load
The maximum sustained request rate per second before throttling
quiz.explanation: Durability measures the probability that stored data is not corrupted or permanently lost. Eleven nines means statistically losing one object per 100 billion objects stored per year. S3 achieves this via automatic replication across multiple AZs. Durability and availability (service uptime) are separate SLAs.

quiz.question: A startup needs 500 servers for a 2-hour load test, then will shut them all down. Why is cloud IaaS economically ideal for this?
options: Cloud servers run at 500x the speed of equivalent on-premises hardware
Cloud providers guarantee zero network latency for test workloads
Pay-as-you-go means they pay only for 2 hours of usage with no hardware procurement cost
IaaS includes built-in load testing software and reporting dashboards
quiz.explanation: Purchasing 500 physical servers for a 2-hour test would require large capital expenditure. Cloud pay-as-you-go charges only for the duration of use — roughly 1000 instance-hours. After terminating the instances, no further cost accrues. This makes ephemeral burst capacity economically viable.

quiz.question: What is the PRIMARY difference between Multi-AZ and Multi-Region deployments?
options: Multi-AZ uses database replicas; Multi-Region uses object storage only
Multi-AZ protects against data-center-level failures in one geography; Multi-Region protects against full regional outages and serves global users with lower latency
Multi-AZ is only available on AWS; Multi-Region is available on all cloud providers
Multi-AZ requires manual failover; Multi-Region failover is always automatic
quiz.explanation: AZs are separate data centers within the same geographic region — Multi-AZ handles local hardware failures. Regions are geographically distinct (different countries or continents) — Multi-Region defends against regional disasters, regulatory requirements, and serves globally distributed users with lower latency.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the customer's responsibility in a PaaS deployment such as AWS Elastic Beanstalk?
options: Patching the underlying OS on the servers running the application
Managing the web server (Nginx/Apache) configuration and version
Application code, its dependencies, data stored in the app, and IAM access policies
Replacing failed physical hardware in the data center
quiz.explanation: In PaaS, the provider manages the OS, runtime, web server, and infrastructure layer. The customer is responsible for their application code and its security, the data stored within the application, and IAM configuration controlling access to cloud resources.
